title: Each official: money from lobbyists’ circles, by channel
question: For each supervisor, mayor and other elected official, how much came from lobbyists’ circles, through which channel, and what share of everything they raised is it?
finding: For 52 officials and candidates the four channels together come to $5.5 million since 2010: $898,128 into their own committees, $533,828 as the circle’s share of independent spending for them, $4.1 million paid to others at their request and $29,547 in gifts and travel. Money into their own committees is 1.9% of the $47.6 million those committees took in (typical official 2.3%; highest Katy Tang, 11.4%). The largest totals: Edwin Lee ($4.1 million), London N. Breed ($410,420), Daniel Lurie ($118,098), Mark Farrell ($102,695).
how: Officials are everyone the roll calls show holding a Board seat (the site’s “Votes, appeals and hearings” page) plus anyone with a campaign committee for City office whom lobbyists reported contacting ten or more times at an elected office. Own committees: itemized contributions from the circle, as in the firm screen, to every committee the person controls (City office; party-committee and other seats shown apart). Independent spending: the circle’s proportional share from the committee screen. Requested payments, gifts and travel: from the gifts screen. The share divides own-committee money by all contributions those committees reported since 2010, itemized and unitemized. “From givers who lobbied them” counts circle money whose firm or client reported contacting that official within two years either side.
limits: Lobbying is registered, and so is giving by a lobbyist’s clients and colleagues. These sums are a small part of most officials’ fundraising, and the largest recipients are those who ran the most expensive citywide races. Independent spending is not under the candidate’s control. Requested payments went to charities and public programs. Public financing and loans are not in the denominator. An official can sponsor or vote for something a donor wants because the official already favoured it; a donor can give to an official because of what the official already stands for. A private payment for an official act cannot be seen in any of these records, and nothing here says one was made.
